issues.title: Non-reentrant signal handlers accessing shared state
issues.description: The interrupt_handler() and fatal_signal_handler() functions access shared global state (linux_thread_pool_t) without proper synchronization. While sigaction() is used with SA_SIGINFO, there's potential for race conditions if signals arrive while shared structures are being modified.
issues.suggested_fix: Use atomic operations for all shared state accessed from signal handlers. Consider using signalfd() instead of traditional signal handlers for better synchronization. Ensure all accesses to interrupt_message are atomic.

issues.title: mutex_t::is_locked() lacks synchronization
issues.description: The is_locked() method returns the 'locked' boolean member without any synchronization. In multi-threaded scenarios with cross_thread_mutex_t usage, this could lead to torn reads and undefined behavior.
issues.suggested_fix: Add proper memory ordering (e.g., std::atomic<bool> or acquire-release semantics) or document that this method is only safe on the mutex's home thread. Consider marking the method as deprecated since mutex_t is already deprecated.

issues.title: one_waiter_cond_t::wait_ordered() missing spurious wakeup handling
issues.description: The wait_ordered() method waits on a condition without checking the predicate (pulsed_) in a loop. While the class documentation states it's for single waiters, spurious wakeups can still occur in POSIX threads.
issues.suggested_fix: Add a loop to re-check the condition after waking up: while (!pulsed_) { waiter_ = coro_t::self(); coro_t::wait(); }

issues.title: auto_drainer_t refcount modification without synchronization
issues.description: The incref() and decref() methods assert thread but don't have any explicit synchronization. While they assert they're on the correct thread, if the drainer is ever rethreaded or accessed from multiple threads, this could lead to race conditions.
issues.suggested_fix: Use std::atomic<int> for refcount if there's any possibility of cross-thread access, or add stronger assertions/documentation about thread safety.

issues.title: worker_cnt atomic operations may lack proper memory ordering
issues.description: The worker_cnt is declared as std::atomic<int> which is good, but the increment/decrement operations use default memory ordering (sequential consistency). While safe, this may be overkill and could impact performance. More importantly, worker_cnt is read without synchronization in dealloc_blocking().
issues.suggested_fix: Consider using memory_order_relaxed for these counters if they're only used for statistics. Ensure reads in dealloc_blocking() use proper atomic loads.

issues.title: Use of volatile for synchronization
issues.description: Using volatile bool for do_shutdown is not the correct way to achieve thread synchronization in C++. volatile does not provide memory ordering guarantees or atomicity.
issues.suggested_fix: Replace with std::atomic<bool> with appropriate memory ordering (e.g., std::atomic<bool> do_shutdown{false}; and use load/store with memory_order_release/acquire).

issues.title: Signal handler callback modifies volatile bool without atomicity
issues.description: The cancel_subscription_t writes to a volatile bool from a signal handler context. While volatile prevents caching, it doesn't guarantee atomicity on all platforms.
issues.suggested_fix: Use std::atomic<bool> or std::atomic_flag for cancellation flags accessed from signal handlers.

issues.title: THREAD_LOCAL macro may cause issues with THREADED_COROUTINES
issues.description: The thread_initial_fiber variable is declared as THREAD_LOCAL but accessed from assembly/context switching code. If THREADED_COROUTINES is defined, the implementation changes significantly.
issues.suggested_fix: Ensure proper synchronization when THREADED_COROUTINES is enabled. Add static assertions to verify TLS implementation matches build configuration.

issues.title: Potential lock ordering issue in push_messages()
issues.description: The push_messages() method acquires spinlocks on multiple threads' incoming_messages_lock_ in a loop. If multiple threads call push_messages() concurrently, this could lead to lock ordering violations or deadlocks.
issues.suggested_fix: Establish a global lock ordering (e.g., by thread ID) and always acquire locks in that order. Consider using a try-lock mechanism with backoff.

issues.title: cross_thread_mutex_t co_lock() may block with spinlock held
issues.description: The co_lock() function releases the spinlock before calling coro_t::wait(), which is correct. However, if an exception occurs or the coroutine is terminated unexpectedly, the mutex state could become inconsistent.
issues.suggested_fix: Add exception safety guarantees and ensure the mutex state is always consistent even if coroutines are terminated unexpectedly.

issues.title: pmap outstanding counter shared across coroutines
issues.description: The 'outstanding' counter is shared across multiple coroutines spawned by pmap. While coroutines on the same thread don't run truly concurrently, the lack of explicit synchronization could be problematic if the compiler optimizes aggressively.
issues.suggested_fix: Use std::atomic<int64_t> for the outstanding counter or document that this is safe due to cooperative multitasking.

issues.title: extproc_spawner_t::instance is a global singleton without synchronization
issues.description: The instance pointer is accessed from multiple threads without explicit synchronization. While the comment suggests it should only be accessed before/after thread pool creation, there's no enforcement.
issues.suggested_fix: Use std::atomic<extproc_spawner_t*> with std::memory_order_acquire/release semantics, or use std::call_once for initialization.

recommendations.description: Audit all uses of 'volatile' for thread synchronization and replace with std::atomic where appropriate. The C++11 memory model makes volatile inappropriate for synchronization.
Review all signal handlers for async-signal-safety. Consider using signalfd() on Linux instead of traditional signal handlers to avoid async-signal-safety issues.
Establish and document a global lock ordering hierarchy to prevent deadlocks. This is especially important for cross-thread operations.
Audit all atomic operations for proper memory ordering. Use std::memory_order_relaxed only where appropriate, otherwise use acquire/release semantics.
Add thread-safety documentation to all concurrency primitives. Document which methods are safe from which threads.

architecture_notes.threading_model: RethinkDB uses a cooperative coroutine model with a thread pool. Each thread has its own coroutine scheduler. Cross-thread operations use message passing through linux_message_hub_t.
key_primitives: cross_thread_mutex_t - Mutex usable across threads with spinlock protection
safety_mechanisms: home_thread_mixin_t - Asserts operations on correct thread
ASSERT_NO_CORO_WAITING - Prevents yielding in critical sections
